research_tasks: Research log (2026-10-15, first run, mode create, empty baseline, no prior evidence, no research notes file). No existing draft, page or research brief for Mike Faist was found under any name in src/blog/people or docs/content-analysis/research. Not open-case eligible: his professional career began in 2011 (Newsies), he was Tony-nominated in 2017 and his film breakthrough was 2021, with a decade of interviews; the type question is hard, but the record is not thin. Opened 37 sources (S01-S37) and failed to open 3 (S38-S40). Read in full: Another Man 2024 (S01), GQ 2026 (S02), the PBS American Masters transcript (S03), the New York Times 2021 Q&A (S04), the Washington Post 2021 profile (S05), Esquire UK 2024 (S06), Cultured 2026 (S07), Interview 2026 and 2017 (S08, S09), Forbes 2026 (S10), and local-Whisper transcripts of eight videos from 2016-2026 (S16-S23, about 25,000 words). Evidence was gathered before a type was chosen. A Four reading formed from the 2021-2024 print record and was then tested against the 2017 BUILD and 2022 BAFTA transcripts, which strengthened the Six rival (anxiety before every project). Outcome: status ready, standard format, Type 4 at medium confidence, Type 6 the strongest rival, Type 9 live, contested_typing flagged so the six-role jury reviews it.

Transcript fidelity. YouTube caption downloads and the transcript API were blocked from this machine during the run (HTTP 429, then an IP block). Audio was downloaded with yt-dlp using the mweb player client and transcribed locally with whisper.cpp (ggml medium.en). Only the Spielberg featurette (S22) was second-transcribed (small.en); both versions garble the middle of his sentence, so quote only "a deep feeler as a human being and as an actor" and "considering delaying the movie" unless someone checks it by ear. Before printing any verbatim quote from S16-S23 or S37, re-listen at the timestamp or second-transcribe; punctuation and filler words are machine-made. Scratch files (may not survive to later stages): audio in /tmp/mike-faist-research/audio, transcripts in /tmp/mike-faist-research/tx and /tmp/mike-faist-research/whisper_cpp, print text in /tmp/mike-faist-research/txt. Every excerpt in this file was machine-checked against those saved texts before writing (0 mismatches).

Access workarounds. S04 (New York Times; the reader proxy was blocked) and S10 (Forbes; 403/CAPTCHA) were opened through Wayback raw captures (web.archive.org/web/<year>id_/<url>; the Forbes capture is gzip-encoded). S11, S12, S13, S14, S34 and S35 were also opened through Wayback. S24 and S36 (TV Insider) and S31 (IBDB) were opened through r.jina.ai after 403s. Not independent: Page Six and DNYUZ republish S02; People (S33) aggregates S01 and S09; Esquire Australia republishes S06.

Do-not-use list. (1) Do not name his 2016 girlfriend (S17), his birth mother or his half-brothers (S09); no speculation about his sexuality or relationships, which the Rodent Man and queer-role coverage invite. (2) Do not call the 2015 "dark, depressed place" depression or any diagnosis (C13). (3) The teenage pot-selling is his joke plus the writer’s paraphrase in one profile (S01, C05); if used at all, attribute it and keep it light. (4) Do not print a Challengers weight figure: sources give just under 15 lb (Little White Lies), 20 lb of muscle (S01) and 30 lb (Wikipedia, Cultured). (5) Family details conflict: grandmother (his mother, S01) vs great-grandmother (him, S03) for the relative with dementia; grandfather died "a month later" (S01) vs "within three weeks" (S02) of his father; his mother practised law for 40 years (S01) while the family ran a real-estate business (S09). Attribute; do not reconcile. (6) His mother is Julie in S01, where she speaks, and Julia in People and Wikipedia. (7) The "two-year" break means no new production between the East of Eden shoot and August 2026; he still did 2024 promotion and the 2024 Met Gala, so do not say he vanished from public view entirely. (8) "Death has long weighed heavily on Mike’s mind," "It was theatre that saved him" and the invisibility motive are the Another Man writer’s interpretations. (9) No reason is known for the Anna Christie withdrawal; do not guess. (10) His 2026 "dread" answer is one rehearsed line repeated in four outlets (C17); present it once, not as four observations. (11) Page Six’s "premieres Friday" is wrong; East of Eden premiered Thursday, October 1, 2026.

Unopened or set aside. Could not open: the Scottish Daily Mail’s January 2022 interview (S38, paywalled; may give his parents’ professions), Jeff Nichols on the CinePie podcast (S39, German, cited by Wikipedia for the screenplay), the Columbus Dispatch’s December 2021 hometown profile (S40, 404), BAFTA Film Sessions 2022 (403). Read and not listed because they add nothing or attribution is too loose: a 48-minute 2017 Broadwaysted drinking podcast re-uploaded by a fan account (unlabelled crosstalk), the AwardsDaily 2022 video (character analysis only), Out and Little White Lies 2024 (short junket answers), the Boston Globe 2024 Challengers item, NPR’s Challengers review, L’Eclaireur (French aggregation), Netflix’s 3-minute "Creating the Character" featurette (background on Charles only). sources.title: Mike Faist Pulls Back the Curtain
sources.speaker: Mike Faist, profiled over two days in Ohio by Ted Stansfield (Another Man); also his mother Julie, his cousin John, his aunt Cheri and his roommate Dan
sources.locator: Online feature, Summer/Autumn 2024 issue (on sale April 25, 2024). Paragraphs on the drive to Woodville (father Kurt died December 12 of a blood clot after three years of pulmonary fibrosis); cousin John; the move to New York at 17; the Postmates encounter with Ben Platt; Dear Evan Hansen research; West Side Story as "vessel"; the Sufjan Stevens drive ("I don’t want to do this as a job"); the flight-or-invisibility debate; Waffle House breakfast on Challengers; his mother Julie on his childhood; the Massey’s dinner where he cries about his parents.
sources.excerpt: Since then, research has been my way to feel more secure, to feel like I am prepared. Even if you have to throw it all away in the end. [...] It felt like: I’m not me right now, I’m being used to tell the story in the best way possible. I don’t know how to explain it, it was like I had no control over the situation. It was like being used as a vessel, and that was the best feeling ever. [...] “I don’t want to do this as a job,” Mike says at one point, staring ahead at the road before him. “For me, it’s deeper than that.” [...] I have a strange relationship to acting: I really love it, but at the same time I get so exhausted by it. And I fall in and out of love with it on a pretty regular basis. [...] I only really want to do pieces that come from a place of love [...] it’s coming from that place of ‘I’m free, I’m liberated, I’m the most authentic I can be.’ [...] “I’m going to be Gene Kelly one day,” he told his mum [...] it’s here that he returned to in February 2021 when his father got sick, to be closer to his family. [...] The designer later asked Mike to appear in a Loewe campaign (for the SS24 pre-collection) and while Mike was initially reticent, it was soon apparent that Jonathan wasn’t going to take no for an answer. [...] And I fall in and out of love with it on a pretty regular basis.
sources.context: The richest single source: the writer spent two days with Faist, his family and his high-school friends shortly after his father and grandfather died, and before the Challengers press tour. Interpretive lines are the writer's ("I suspect that the real reason is Mike’s discomfort with the public position"; "Death has long weighed heavily on Mike’s mind"); keep them attributed or out. Also the source for: he was "terrified" moving to New York at 17 and his father drove him; food stamps and a peanut-butter diet; he "remembers bumping into the actor (and Dear Evan Hansen co-star) Ben Platt when he was on a job for Postmates ... and feeling so ashamed that he pretended he was doing something else" (writer's paraphrase); Dan calls teenage Mike "A loose cannon" and Mike corrects "Eccentric ... Floaty and an idiot"; a teacher barred him from school plays over his behaviour "which is when he decided to make a change"; "selling a bit of pot" as a teenager (writer's paraphrase; "I think I sold them some pot though" is his joke); his mother Julie: "He was born an adult ... At six, he told me he wanted to start saving for college. At six!"; his mother practised law for 40 years (conflicts with the family real-estate business in S09; both may be true); he chose invisibility over flight, for "random acts of kindness, like watering an old lady’s garden" (writer's paraphrase); he was "dreading the Challengers press tour and admits he was even dreading this interview a bit"; "insecurities that sometimes flare up about his being a small-town boy from Ohio" (writer's paraphrase); he pulls a bandana over his mouth "when he is feeling shy" (writer's interpretation); cousin John: "He was a quiet young man. And he’s always been very committed to his family."; on his parents, "his voice cracking and his eyes suddenly smarting with tears": "That’s something that physically hurts me". His mother says the dementia-afflicted relative who watched old films was his grandmother; in S03 he says great-grandmother. Says his grandfather died "A month later" after his father; S02 says within three weeks.

sources.title: Mike Faist Returns to the Spotlight With ‘East of Eden’
sources.speaker: Mike Faist, interviewed walking his dog in Prospect Park by Raymond Ang (GQ); with Zoe Kazan, Tony Kushner, Florence Pugh and Justin Kuritzkes
sources.locator: GQ Hype cover story, interview in August 2026. Paragraphs on the two-year step back after Challengers; Kushner on roles he turned down; Kazan on his privacy and the "hermit crab"; "This is the part that I don’t know how to do"; Kazan on meeting twice before he agreed; Netflix paying for an extra episode; father and grandfather; "living in the Matrix"; Kushner on his screenplay; rehearsals for an unannounced project; Kushner on "what he’s fought hard to get out of"; closing line. Also: the "public gaze" exchange after the stamina quote; the rehearsals/financing paragraph; Kuritzkes on Sgt. Rock; the Charles Trask "against type" and Netflix-episode paragraphs.
sources.excerpt: It became very apparent to me, there’s a moment of just needing to recalibrate probably for myself [...] I think a lot of people will do one thing and then they double down and they get onto the next thing. They want this momentum [...] I don’t think that I have that kind of stamina. I’m not necessarily a marathon runner. [...] Look, the truth is, it’s a lot easier for me to put on a character and be in front of the world than be me [...] There’s a privacy to Mike that I feel, even having worked with him and spent time with him, that I am very careful not to push on, because it feels so important to who he is [...] I just need to know that this is right for me, because when I jump in, I jump in 100%. If you have me, you’re going to have me 100%. [...] if you want to get to know me, just watch my movies. [...] Was it the grind of promoting a movie all over the world? “It’s the public gaze,” he says. “It’s this: Before, you’re able to walk outside, you’re able to go to your neighborhood coffee shop, able to chat with your normal person, and you could kind of be whoever you wanted to be. I really loved operating in the world with anonymity and being able to talk to strangers without them knowing who I was, because for some reason that was an ability for me to be even more honest with them.” [...] “There’s things that pop up and for whatever reason, they don’t happen because of the industry and financing,” he explains. “There’s no control in this industry.” [...] “That’s hard with actors, because you can also become an actor who says no to a lot,” Kushner says. “But I’m intrigued by what he’s decided to do and what he has decided not to do and what he’s fought hard to get out of.” [...] Sgt. Rock was very much a superhero movie that was about everyday heroes, humans, normal people [...] In the series, Faist is playing against type, taking on Charles Trask [...] “Netflix was like, ‘We love him so much. We’ll pay for another episode,’” says Kazan, who found a way to write Faist into a later episode.
sources.context: The fullest account of the 2024-2026 withdrawal and the most independent testimony in the record. Kazan (showrunner, East of Eden): "There’s something about Mike that reads to me like a hermit crab or something. There’s this shell on the outside and you can’t tell what’s inside. And there’s a softness to him, but there’s also this kind of toughness ... Like, steely."; "It’s really admirable to me that Mike is pursuing a life that feels authentic to him." Kushner (screenwriter, West Side Story) on roles friends offered after 2021: "I think in both cases he turned them down ... the stuff that they were asking just didn’t feel right to him at the moment, and it had nothing to do with size of the role"; "I’m intrigued by what he’s decided to do and what he has decided not to do and what he’s fought hard to get out of"; his screenplay "a very, very interesting, beautifully written script". Pugh on his supporting role. Facts: he dropped out of Anna Christie two months after it was announced; Sgt. Rock with Guadagnino fell through; moved to Ohio in 2021 to help care for his father, who had pulmonary fibrosis; father and grandfather "passed within three weeks of each other"; "All the men have passed ... It’s my sister, my mom and my grandmother, and me."; in August 2026 he was "about to enter rehearsals for the first production he’s worked on since East of Eden", unnamed. On construction: a 2017 line, "Once it’s all over, I’ll go back to construction work," which he now calls "the narrative of my life"; renovation is "very grounding. It’s real. It’s tangible." Lighter lines: on the Rodent Man label, "One hundo p!"; on Oh, Mary!, "I would rock Mary Todd." Page Six and DNYUZ republished excerpts (not independent). Also quoted in the draft: Kuritzkes on Sgt. Rock, "more or less in prep" when it fell apart ("You can ask DC Studios"); "I'm just proud that I'm able to go on a walk with you and do this. For me, that's a big step."; "I'm always saying ... if you want to get to know me, just watch my movies." Edit-stage note (2026-10-15): the "public gaze" answer follows the interviewer question "Was it the grind of promoting a movie all over the world?"; the "industry and financing" answer follows the August 2026 rehearsals paragraph and precedes the Sgt. Rock example. Kushner's "says no to a lot" / "fought hard to get out of" remark sits in the closing passage about whether the industry "will continue to wait for Mike Faist" and names no project. GQ also: "In 2021, just after West Side Story, Faist packed up his belongings in New York and moved back to Ohio to help care for his ailing father"; "His father and grandfather passed within three weeks of each other, right before the release of Challengers"; "Faist thinks he signed on to East of Eden because the work provided a feeling of home."

sources.title: Mike Faist Embraces the Unknown (American Masters: Creative Spark podcast)
sources.speaker: Mike Faist, interviewed by Joe Skinner (PBS American Masters)
sources.locator: Full published transcript (page dated October 2, 2026; also on YouTube as xjilKHdJkGk, uploaded the same day; one PBS listing gives an air date of October 1). Answers on: dread; moving to New York at 17 ("Maybe I’ll be good one day"); "hell yes and oh shit"; Zoe Kazan steering the ship; the older he gets "the more embarrassed I get to be an actor"; painful boots and solitary weekends on the set; Michael Shannon on The Bikeriders ("all I had to do was just be the observer"); "No one has the answers"; telling Pugh and Abbott "I’m just going to be quiet"; "acting is just constantly giving"; the closing answer on why he keeps going ("I’m an addict").
sources.excerpt: I remember really genuinely feeling that way. I still feel that way. Maybe I’ll be good one day. [...] It’s that feeling of hell yes and oh shit, you know? [...] That helps any sort of anxieties because it’s like, well, someone’s steering the ship. Someone knows what they’re doing . [...] And it’s funny, the older I get, the more embarrassed I get to be an actor. [...] And I just remember letting them both know, I was like, “Hey, just so you know, I’m just going to be quiet. I just want to be over here. I’m just going to be off in a corner.” I feel like I need that [...] No one has the answers. It really does require a community of people to build a thing because it’s just so hard [...] I don’t know why I keep going, ’cause I’m an addict. [...] You know, she had a really specific point of view, which is really what you want. You know, you want a director and a leader that’s going to say, “No, we’re doing this. Let’s get specific. Let’s get clear on what we want to do.” That helps any sort of anxieties because it’s like, well, someone’s steering the ship. [...] I remember saying when I was leaving that I was just really excited to get better. [...] I still feel that way. Maybe I’ll be good one day. That’d be cool.
sources.context: A 44-minute craft conversation published the day after the East of Eden premiere; the longest first-person source in the record and the least promotional in tone. He calls himself "a nerd" who likes talking about acting and apologises for it ("Sorry, you know. I don’t know. Sorry. I know."). On Florence Pugh and Christopher Abbott switching on and off: "I’m not good enough is the truth." On The Bikeriders: "I chose that job because all I had to do was just be the observer." On why he became an actor: watching Singin’ in the Rain in the basement with his great-grandmother, who had dementia ("Can you do this for a living?"). On what keeps him going: "part of me feels like ... ‘Oh, well, I don’t really have anything else to contribute.’ This is maybe the only thing that I’m kind of good at, maybe."; "I don’t want to hold it so tightly because I think if you hold it too tightly, maybe it’ll die." The "steering the ship" answer is his account of saying yes to Kazan's East of Eden offer. "I still feel that way" answers a question about dread and recalls the 17-year-old who was "really excited to get better".

sources.title: Mike Faist Isn’t Sure About This Whole Acting Thing
sources.speaker: Mike Faist, interviewed in Park Slope by Elisabeth Vincentelli (The New York Times); with Lauren Oliver and Jessica Sula
sources.locator: Edited Q&A ahead of the Panic premiere. Opened through the Wayback Machine raw capture (web.archive.org/web/2021id_/...); the live page was not reachable. Intro paragraphs (driving the country with Austin, writing a screenplay, turning down offers, selling his Brooklyn apartment; "protective self-deprecation"); Jessica Sula on the trailer; answers to "Why aren’t you in the upcoming ‘Dear Evan Hansen’ movie?", "what are you lining up?" and "Which is what?".
sources.excerpt: I feel like I couldn’t do it. I started that when I was, like, 21, and was with it for five or six years. When you’re doing eight shows a week, it very much turns into relying on your technique and the job of it. And the show was such a zeitgeisty thing. It really took a lot out of me, and I didn’t really have it in me anymore. [...] It’s really crazy, but it was transcendental: either I didn’t feel like I was myself, or I was the most authentic version of myself. I can’t really tell which one. Having gone from having no money, wanting to just be a working actor — I don’t want to just be a working actor anymore. [...] I can’t tell if I hate acting or if I love it too much. It’s not like I don’t plan on doing it. I just don’t want to follow the trajectory of what the industry wants me to do. [...] Put on a cape and wear a mask. I need to take more agency because no one’s going to do it for me. [...] I would like to ultimately be of service and of use; that’s when I feel at my best. [...] Having gone from having no money, wanting to just be a working actor — I don’t want to just be a working actor anymore. I had that experience. [...] The pandemic nearly killed us and — what, I just want to be an actor? That’s ridiculous. [Laughs.] I don’t care enough. It’s a weird thing: I can’t tell if I hate acting or if I love it too much. [...] I’m going to hang out with my family in Ohio and then start to figure out where I’m going to go.
sources.context: Written seven months before West Side Story opened, during the period he later describes as a pandemic-era road trip. The reporter: "He spent some of the past year driving around the country with Austin and writing a screenplay. He has been turning down offers and is now selling his Brooklyn apartment and heading back to Ohio."; "he laughed a lot in what seemed to be protective self-deprecation". Jessica Sula (Panic co-star): when shooting resumed in Texas, "Faist chose to live in a trailer on a plot of land with his rescue dog, Austin"; "He’s just so fabulously ridiculous and wonderful." Also: "I don’t care enough." and "It [expletive] me up." (about West Side Story, "in the best of ways"). A LiveJournal repost of the same text was also read and matches. The reporter also predicts the film "should put him on Hollywood's speed dial when it debuts in December" (quoted in the draft as "on Hollywood's speed dial").

sources.title: Mike Faist was a ‘blue-collar working theater actor.’ Now, he’s a standout in Spielberg’s first musical.
sources.speaker: Thomas Floyd (The Washington Post, syndicated by Stars and Stripes); testimony from Tony Kushner and Michael Greif; Mike Faist
sources.locator: Paragraphs 2-3 (Kushner on the mural), the Greif quote, Kushner on research ("gobbled all that stuff up"), the gun scene, and the closing quotes on "passion and love".
sources.excerpt: It was something that he needed to do because he felt terribly about what his character had just done, and he needed to do something to make himself feel okay about it. [...] He always took extremely seriously his responsibility of representing this kid in that kind of emotional despair and that kind of crisis. [...] I wanted to morph. I wanted to change. I wanted to create an environment, not just for myself but for other people, where we didn’t have to ... [...] If it’s anything short of that, I don’t know if it’s worth it. I was just really wrestling with this idea of, ‘Do I love acting or do I hate it?’ And the truth is that I think I love it too much. I really do. [...] Shortly after Faist exited the show in the summer of 2018, he sent his audition tape for another tormented character: the pithy but pitiable Riff. That November, he was performing in Steven Levenson’s off-Broadway play “Days of Rage” when he got the call to audition.
sources.context: Independent named testimony. Kushner's favourite memory of the shoot: after the Jets splashed paint on a Puerto Rican flag mural, "One of the people washing it was Mike ... it really wasn’t in any way done for display." Greif directed Dear Evan Hansen. Kushner on the unscripted moment when Riff presses his temple to the gun barrel: "What Mike came up with in that moment ... is the whole character in this one little gesture." Faist: "I’m a blue-collar working theater actor and this is a big, buzzy Hollywood production."; on recognition: "it’s not, at the end of the day, why I do what I do. For me, it has to come from a place of passion and love." Asked about the New York Times comments, he says "There’s still so much more to say ... and there’s still so much more to do."

sources.title: Mike Faist on The Bikeriders, Challengers and Hollywood Fatigue
sources.speaker: Mike Faist, interviewed at Claridge’s the day after the London Challengers premiere by Henry Wong (Esquire UK)
sources.locator: Opening paragraph (planned break after Challengers, "allow myself to be bored"); Bikeriders paragraph ("opposite side of the camera"); paragraph on adoptive parents; tennis paragraph ("I’m far too emotional"); pilot’s licence paragraph ("I think I just get bored"). Republished by Esquire Australia, also read.
sources.excerpt: I viewed myself to be on the opposite side of the camera almost, just sitting there and watching these actors [...] I didn’t have the mental fortitude it requires just to remain tough and keep calm [...] I’m far too emotional. [...] My younger brothers are both pilots [...] And I thought maybe I could do it, too. So I just did it. [...] I think I just get bored [...] After filming wrapped on Challengers [...] Mike Faist [...] decided to take a break. The 32-year-old actor, who splits his time between New York and Ohio, had planned to drive around the US with his dog and spend time with his friends and family, to “allow myself to be bored”, as he puts it. But then, director Jeff Nichols called. [...] “They had their pilot’s licenses, and I was impressed with how young they were. And I thought maybe I could do it, too. So I just did it.”
sources.context: The meeting took place in April 2024, the day after the London Challengers premiere; published June 2024. The writer: Faist had planned to take a break after filming Challengers, to drive around the US with his dog, until Jeff Nichols called about The Bikeriders; Zendaya had got him into photography. Also: "I was nervous about going into that process, because of the Spielberg of it all, and because of the Hollywood of it all" and Spielberg "never made me feel I needed to ask permission to do anything"; "Honestly, who cares about acting?" (asked how he picks roles). States he was raised by adoptive parents.

sources.title: It’s Been Two Years, but Mike Faist Is Back Onscreen in Another Love Triangle
sources.speaker: Mike Faist, interviewed over Zoom by Sophie Lee (Cultured)
sources.locator: Q&A answers: "how this project came to you" (dreadful), "Is there something in a character ... that makes you think, I could do a really good job" (dread, the volcano), "Did you feel like you wanted to take a beat" (noise, two years), "Was it a little bit of a whiplash situation?", "Are you thinking of doing something in that Challengers-esque world again?" (trusting he will know), "Is that sensation ... what you expected" ("doomed to do this"). Also: "What made you sign onto this one?" (honestly Zoe and Florence); "Do you feel like theater is your natural register?" (go back to the theater); writer's intro paragraphs (Riff, Loewe/Met Gala, Charles Trask).
sources.excerpt: I don’t think I ever feel like I can do a good job. But … there’s a fear that kicks in. There’s a feeling of dread, a real dread, and I think it is just because you start to feel that you actually care. The other tiny voice inside of you goes, Oh, don’t do that. Don’t jump into the volcano. Stay up here where it’s safe. But, that’s the thrill of what we get to do. [...] it’s very easy to get swept up in noise. It makes it difficult for me to really listen, just being able to hear myself think, and feel what is right for me. [...] The truth is that Challengers was a lot. It was very overwhelming [...] Oftentimes, I’ve said that I don’t really know how much control I actually have over any of this. [...] Well, It was, honestly Zoe and Florence. Florence was a producer for a few years [...] You know, there really isn’t a lot of thought. [...] Yes, maybe there was an aspect of trying to tune everything out and, looking back, it was two years [without acting]. Maybe there was an aspect of me just trying to say, I’m going to pull back from all of this, and allow things to be quiet. [...] I would love to go back to the theater at some point. Absolutely. [...] I remain open and optimistic that I’ll be able to find my way back. I haven’t been back on an American stage in close to 10 years. [...] It was very jarring. It was a whiplash situation.
sources.context: Interview conducted in September 2026, during the East of Eden press cycle. Also: "I love being an actor, I love telling stories, and I love investigating characters and excavating everything that I can out of myself in order to serve the role."; "I’m kind of just allowing that when the opportunities come, I probably am trusting that I will know whether something is actually right for me or not. It’s kind of like dating"; "I think, unfortunately, I’m doomed to do this."; on Pugh, "I really saw it as my job to make her feel as uncomfortable as possible" and "I really felt like I met my match." The writer notes he brushed off the hiatus question ("You know, there really isn’t a lot of thought."). Also quoted in the draft (same answer as the noise passage): "Maybe there was an aspect of me just trying to say, I'm going to pull back from all of this, and allow things to be quiet." Writer's framing also used: Faist ended up playing "the much-lauded Riff, leader of the Jets"; "(In 2024, Anderson put Faist in both a Loewe campaign and on the Met Gala carpet in a custom look.)"; "Faist plays Charles Trask, a quiet farmer who’s dangerous when provoked." "You know, there really isn’t a lot of thought" was his first answer to whether he wanted to take a beat after Challengers and The Bikeriders.

sources.title: A Reluctant Interview Between Mike Faist and Jonathan Anderson
sources.speaker: Mike Faist in conversation with the designer Jonathan Anderson (Interview)
sources.locator: Conversation recorded September 17, 2026, in Paris. Faist’s turns beginning "No, the reality is that I don’t like doing interviews", "Part of the reason I don’t like doing interviews", "I get embarrassed too", and the closing exchange ("I think I got away with it").
sources.excerpt: Part of the reason I don’t like doing interviews is that I actually feel a lot more comfortable being a character than I do being myself in the public eye. I feel a lot braver, quite frankly, to be someone else. [...] I get embarrassed too. I’m embarrassed to do this interview. [...] After I read it, I felt extreme excitement, empathy, understanding to a degree, and dread. [...] Except I was able to actually pretty much interview you. I think I got away with it. [...] Part of the reason I don’t like doing interviews is that I actually feel a lot more comfortable being a character than I do being myself in the public eye. [...] ANDERSON: [...] I do feel there is me on and there’s me off. [...] You do become insecure of the idea of yourself as yourself.
sources.context: A friend-to-friend conversation (they met on Challengers, where Anderson was costume designer), so it is less guarded but also playful. He opens by turning the questions back on Anderson ("It’s much more interesting to hear things about you.") and closes by claiming he interviewed Anderson instead. Anderson: "he was such a friendly person"; "You’re just a modest person, Mike." Faist: "I wanted to move to New York specifically because I wanted to follow in the lineage of James Dean, Brando, Newman, and De Niro."; joined East of Eden "because I wanted it to be a part of my evolution as a human being, my personal growth"; "I’m doing the only thing I’ve ever wanted to do."

sources.title: Discovery: Mike Faist
sources.speaker: Mike Faist, interviewed by Annie Powers (Interview)
sources.locator: Intro paragraphs (summers of construction work for his parents’ real estate business); sections "GROWING UP ON OLD FILMS", "THE FIRST JOB", "SECRET TALENT", "THE EVOLUTION OF CONNOR MURPHY", "LEARNING TO FLY".
sources.excerpt: I dropped out of the [American Musical and Dramatic Academy]. I was basically too nervous and scared to audition for anything afterwards, so a friend of mine at the time dragged me kicking and screaming to an audition for White Christmas in Springboro, Ohio at this dinner theater, and I ended up booking it. [...] that gave me enough confidence to finally go and say, “I can actually do this.” [...] I’m adopted, and I met my birth mom right when I was about to move to New York. [...] Christopher took me up on a flight, and I was thinking, “Hey, I can do this! That’s how we can bond!” It was really crazy and really impulsive. [...] And now we bond as a family in a way, there. [...] they don’t want people to see them because if we allow ourselves to be seen, actually seen, and allow [ourselves] to be vulnerable, then we lose the game. [...] Teens don’t want to let people know how they are actually feeling. I think that’s where this generation is, and where everyone feels marginalized and displaced a little bit. [...] I’m adopted, and I met my birth mom right when I was about to move to New York. I was 17 when I met her and her side of the family. They are a family of pilots. [...] “Hey, I can do this! That’s how we can bond!” It was really crazy and really impulsive. [...] And now we bond as a family in a way, there.
sources.context: Published during the Dear Evan Hansen Broadway run, weeks before his Tony nomination. Also: "I was always very imaginative as a kid; I was always playing pretend. I was always the hero in the story"; writes short stories and was planning an Ohio playwrights’ festival; his research on suicide-attempt survivors through livethroughthis.org; "Gene Kelly was definitely the guy, I think, that I wanted to emulate". Names his half-brother; do not print the name. Interview also identifies "Evan (Ben Platt)". Do not name birth-family members (do-not-use list).

sources.title: Netflix’s ‘East Of Eden’ Pushed Mike Faist Past The Fear To Play Charles Trask
sources.speaker: Mike Faist, interviewed by Olivia Singh (Forbes contributor)
sources.locator: Direct fetch and the reader proxy were blocked (403/CAPTCHA); opened through the Wayback Machine raw capture (web.archive.org/web/2026id_/...). Paragraph after Zoe Kazan approached him; paragraph on "see and be seen"; final section "What’s Next For Mike Faist After ‘East Of Eden’?".
sources.excerpt: There’s two things that go through your mind [...] There’s the ‘Hell yeah, let’s do this and let’s get to work.’ And then the other one is fear, because you don’t want to mess up. That’s the reality. And honestly, that is kind of the only feeling that I’m really searching for within any of this. You want things that are exciting to you and that are going to push you, and also that terrify you. [...] I can’t believe that I’m excited about this and I can’t believe how terrified I am to do it. [...] Then, in Steven Spielberg’s 2021 West Side Story remake, Faist starred as Riff, the impulsive but charismatic and loyal leader of the Jets gang, and earned a BAFTA nomination for his performance.
sources.context: A premiere-day feature built around the same excitement-and-fear answer he gives in S03, S07 and S08, so it shows a repeated framing rather than independent behavior. Also on Charles and Cathy: "this desire to see and be seen is a very real thing."; on what is next: "I don’t have too much thought about it".

sources.title: Gahanna native Faist identified emotionally with lead character's dilemma
sources.speaker: Mike Faist, phone interview with Terry Mikesell (The Columbus Dispatch)
sources.locator: Opened through the Wayback Machine raw capture (2021). Paragraphs on the 2015 script for I Can I Will I Did and the closing quotes on proving himself.
sources.excerpt: I was in this dark, depressed place for a little while, and (the play) was in between out-of-town tryouts and off-Broadway when this script came across my desk [...] It was something I needed to do — mostly for myself because it’s almost therapeutic, to liberate myself from those feelings, by lashing out in the film. [...] It’s a strange industry, where you’re constantly having to prove yourself. I’m auditioning all the time still, finding the next project — working, not working, getting a job, not getting a job — all while trying to persuade people that I’m worth it and figuring out what I want to do. [...] But the work is where I get my true satisfaction.
sources.context: Local hometown paper, ahead of a Bexley screening of a small 2017 film about a bullied foster teenager. The reporter writes that in 2015 Dear Evan Hansen "was between a run in Washington, D.C., and opening off-Broadway" and "Faist was afraid that his character was going to be radically altered." On his audition: "If they want me to do this, I’m going to take some liberties with this." "Dark, depressed place" is his everyday phrase, not a diagnosis. Draft note: the article links to the Wayback capture (web.archive.org/web/2021/<url>) because the live dispatch.com URL may not resolve; the source URL above is unchanged.

sources.title: Dear Evan Hansen Star Opens Up About Skipping Social Media — And The Autograph Line
sources.speaker: Mike Faist, interviewed at the MTV News office by Stacey Grant (MTV News)
sources.locator: Opened through the Wayback Machine raw capture (2017); the live URL now redirects. Answers on the autograph line, social media, and running offstage after the computer-lab scene.
sources.excerpt: I very rarely do the autograph line. I just try and keep my head down and show up to work and do my job [...] And, that’s really amazing and I don’t want to take that away from them, by having them meet who I actually am, so I just kind of distance myself a little bit from all of that. [...] I just would hate for that illusion to be broken by having interaction with me, that, maybe, [fans] were expecting something else [...] I’d just run upstairs to my dressing room and I would just be on the floor, on my knees, head in my chair just taking a knee, beyond a minute. Realized very quickly that I was a little unhealthy [...] right after my computer-lab scene with Ben [Platt, who plays Evan]
sources.context: Interview from the first Broadway spring of Dear Evan Hansen. The writer's framing: "Mike Faist is full of life. He’s charming, funny, and completely candid". He signs "maybe twice a week" for repeat customers "to thank them for all their support." Date from the archived page. Draft note: the article links to the Wayback capture (web.archive.org/web/2017/<url>) because the live URL redirects.

sources.title: Gahanna Native and Tony Nominee Mike Faist Brings Inaugural Ohio Artists Gathering to Short North Stage

sources.excerpt: I wanted to bring this work to a city I love and call home, and I also want to show Columbus what’s in their backyard. [...] Reaching diverse voices was very important to me. [...] We want to talk about where theatre can go here and how to get there. We started this thinking about the next five years; this is about building momentum.

He co-directed and starred in a one-man play by his Dear Evan Hansen castmate, joking "cheapest option all around!" No source found for a second year.

sources.title: “Do I have to dance?”: Mike Faist on moving from stage to screen for ‘West Side Story’
sources.speaker: Mike Faist, video interview from outside Columbus with Michael Rosser (Screen International)
sources.locator: Paragraphs on the Riff dance call ("Do I have to dance?"), the Jets and Harrison Coll, and the closing paragraph on the past two years on the road.
sources.excerpt: I asked my agents, ‘Do I have to dance? Can I just do the scene work?’ To which I was told, ‘This is West Side Story.’ I’m not an ensemble dancer [...] I’m not good enough. I had no business being in that room, quite frankly. [...] We were a family. We were a tribe. [...] I definitely want to come back to theatre. I lived in New York for 13 years. It treated me so well, it shaped who I am. But right now, I’m kinda digging the open road. [...] “I’m not an ensemble dancer,” he explains. “I’m not good enough. I had no business being in that room, quite frankly. These were some of the best dancers in the world. So, for me, it was a case of Riff or bust.” [...] Having left New York at the outset of the pandemic and spent much of the past two years travelling around the US in his car, with his dog
sources.context: The writer: "Having left New York at the outset of the pandemic and spent much of the past two years travelling around the US in his car, with his dog". Also: "I remember sitting down with Steven ... and telling him, ‘I was born to do this.’ This was meant to be."; quotes Spielberg secondhand: "Mike Faist is one-of-a-kind ... He can do absolutely anything."

sources.title: Mike Faist On "Dear Evan Hansen" (BUILD Series)
sources.speaker: Mike Faist, live studio interview with an audience Q&A (BUILD Series; host not named in the transcript)
sources.locator: 27:10 video. Transcribed from the audio with local Whisper (medium.en); YouTube captions were blocked. 01:41-02:12 ("I keep fooling everyone"); 09:59-11:06 (dinner theatre, six to eight months without auditioning); 11:06-11:42 (graduated early, "I kinda had to get out"); 12:14-13:17 (parents trusted him); 19:44-20:17 (Evan and Connor and being seen).
sources.excerpt: I had dropped out of the conservatory program that I was going to and I went maybe six, eight months without auditioning for anything 'cause I felt too incapable. I didn't really want to put myself out there. I was too scared, too whatever. And when I booked that, it gave me enough confidence to be like, oh, well I can actually make this happen. [...] I graduated high school a year early to move to New York 'cause I kinda had to get out. [...] You know, I keep fooling everyone. I really have no idea, it works out. [...] They lose too much of themselves if they really allow themselves to be vulnerable and seen through the other person. [...] Then how do you keep landing these parts? - You know, I keep fooling everyone. I really have no idea, it works out. - You're fooling pretty important people though. - Yeah, I guess so, you know? They keep hiring me, it's their prerogative, I guess, yeah.
sources.context: Promotional but long-form, from the first Broadway year of Dear Evan Hansen. Also: the 2015 Washington rewrite of his role "was daunting. It was scary"; his parents "have always trusted and supported me and believed in me 100%" and "trusted that I was making the right decision for me"; as a child his parents found him "too hyperactive". The 2017 self-account here matches S09 (six to eight months frozen vs "too nervous and scared"). Machine transcript: punctuation and small words are approximate. Both local transcriptions agree on "You know, I keep fooling everyone. I really have no idea, it works out."

sources.title: 'West Side Story' breakout Mike Faist on making Riff his own: 'Start fresh and go back to the text' (Gold Derby)
sources.speaker: Mike Faist, interviewed by Christopher Rosen (Gold Derby)
sources.locator: 27:57 video. Transcribed from the audio with local Whisper (medium.en). 09:19-11:37 (stepping in with the Jets, "Jetivities"); 18:36-19:41 (the gun-barrel idea); 21:50-22:24 (fear Spielberg would make him "a prop"); 24:40-25:51 (staying away from reviews).
sources.excerpt: I have to step in here kind of and do something. [...] I wanted to actually create a family, a brotherhood, a tribe. [...] It wasn't ever my job to scold them or say, "Don't do this, do that," kind of a thing. [...] I was in fear that he would be, you know, not, you know, a dictator. I thought the whole thing would be, you know, Hollywood overproduced. We're an actor. You're just a prop. [...] I stay away from it all because like my job is just for better or worse, like I just have to protect my head space and like stay away from the whole thing. [...] For me, I can't handle it. If you say something nice to me, I'm not gonna be able to handle it
sources.context: Awards-season interview. He also tells the Harrison Coll story (singing the Jet Song as a castmate released his father's ashes) and says the gun-to-the-temple moment was his own idea: "I went over to Steven and Tony. I said, I think I have this idea. Just go with me on it. If you hate it, tell me." On friends who said no one else could have played Riff: "they know me and they know kind of what my skillsets are and they know how I kind of operate in terms of what my particular brand of crazy is." Machine transcript.

sources.title: The time Mike Faist went LARPing with the cast of West Side Story | Tea with BAFTA
sources.speaker: Mike Faist, video call from Ohio with a BAFTA interviewer (first name Robert in the recording)
sources.locator: 10:56 video. Transcribed from the audio with local Whisper (medium.en). 04:27-05:07 (anxiety before every project); 05:41-06:50 (expected to be "the prop"); 09:12-10:23 (Jetivities, LARPing).
sources.excerpt: I tend to get anxious or have a bit of anxiety before every project, no matter what it is. I'm always like, oh my God, what did I sign myself up for? I can't do this. Why did they hire me? What are we thinking? What are we doing here? I always like have this awful, awful thing in my whole body before like starting any sort of project. [...] I'm just gonna have to just wear the costume, stand on my mark and say the line and just be the prop. That's really how I felt going into it. I was nervous about that. [...] I’m always like, oh my God, what did I sign myself up for? I can’t do this. Why did they hire me? What are we thinking? What are we doing here? I always like have this awful, awful thing in my whole body before like starting any sort of project.
sources.context: BAFTA-nomination interview recorded in Ohio ("that's where my family is"). Credits Spielberg with providing "a safe enough space for us to really take ownership". Machine transcript. 09:12-10:23 (both transcriptions): after the first official rehearsal he took the Jets for a drink and "I wanted everyone to come up with an activity and no matter what it was, we all had to do it"; one outing surprised Kyle Allen at his LARPing group. The draft embeds the clip at 04:27-05:07. Second local transcription (whisper/) renders "oh my God, why, what did I sign myself up for?"; the article quotes from "what did I sign myself up for?", where both agree.

sources.title: Mike Faist on East of Eden, that Challengers churros scene and his favourite film line (BBC Radio 1)
sources.speaker: Mike Faist, interviewed by a BBC Radio 1 film presenter (not named in the transcript)
sources.locator: 17:05 video. Transcribed from the audio with local Whisper (medium.en). 00:00 (interviewer reads Spielberg's description); 06:00-06:38 (press is "the most embarrassing thing possible"); 07:09-07:44 ("surround yourself with people ... a lot smarter than you"); 12:09-12:42 (making people laugh in auditions).

[...] I think any time that I could have made someone laugh in the audition, that made me feel good.
sources.context: A deliberately silly press-junket format. The interviewer opens by quoting Spielberg: "a soulful deep thinker, a deep feeler, as a human and as an actor", which corroborates S22. sources.title: Florence Pugh and Mike Faist on 'East of Eden's Surprise Cathy and Charles Reunion (Exclusive)
