claims.claim: Mike Faist was born on January 5, 1992, and raised in Gahanna, Ohio, a suburb of Columbus.
claims.passage: born in 1992 and raised in Gahanna, Ohio
claims.inference: Birth date and place from IBDB (S31), consistent with every printed age (29 in May and December 2021, 30 in early 2022, 32 in April 2024, 34 in September 2026). Gahanna upbringing in S01 and S05. Full date is carried in metadata by C51 and C53; parents and adoption by C52.
claims.alternative: None on the facts.

claims.claim: As a small child he watched Singin' in the Rain on repeat (the family played old MGM musicals for an elderly relative with dementia: his great-grandmother in his 2026 PBS account, his grandmother in Another Man's 2024 account; the edit drops that detail rather than reconcile it), and Another Man reports he told his mother, "I'm going to be Gene Kelly one day."
claims.passage: As a small child Faist watched _Singin' in the Rain_ on repeat. "I'm going to be Gene Kelly one day," he told his mother, Julie
claims.inference: S03: "we took care of my great-grandmother for a period of time who was suffering from dementia ... we put on these old MGM films ... Singin' in the Rain". S01: "His grandmother, who had been living with them at the time and was suffering from dementia, loved old movies"; "'I'm going to be Gene Kelly one day,' he told his mum". Told consistently since 2012 (S35) and 2022 (S15).
claims.alternative: A polished origin story repeated for every press cycle; it shows what he foregrounds, not a cause. The relative is attributed to each speaker, not reconciled.

claims.claim: He graduated from high school a year early, in 2009, and at 17 his father drove him to New York.
claims.passage: He graduated from high school a year early, and at 17 his father drove him to New York.
claims.inference: S01: "When he was 17 years old, in 2009, Mike graduated from high school early ... His father drove him there"; the quote is verbatim (two consecutive quoted pieces around "he remembers"). Graduating early also in S16, S25, S34.
claims.alternative: Struggle-to-New-York is standard actor biography; credible as fact, not as evidence of type.

claims.claim: After dropping out of drama school he "went maybe six, eight months without auditioning for anything 'cause I felt too incapable" (BUILD Series, March 30, 2017; both local transcriptions agree).
claims.passage: he "went maybe six, eight months without auditioning for anything 'cause I felt too incapable."
claims.inference: S16 at 09:59-11:06; wording agrees across the whisper and whisper.cpp transcriptions (the python transcription renders "six eight months" without the comma and "for every anything"). S09 independently: "I was basically too nervous and scared to audition for anything afterwards." The earliest documented instance of a pattern: fear of inadequacy freezes him, and an outside push releases it (C56).
claims.alternative: Ordinary for an 18-year-old who has just quit school. Fits a Six (paralysis resolved by an ally) at least as well as a Four (shame about not being good enough); it does not discriminate on its own.

claims.claim: Another Man reports that in his poor early years in New York he ran into the actor Ben Platt while on a Postmates job and felt "so ashamed that he pretended he was doing something else."
claims.passage: Another Man reports that he ran into the actor Ben Platt while delivering for Postmates and felt "so ashamed that he pretended he was doing something else."
claims.inference: Writer's paraphrase in S01, presented as Faist's memory ("He remembers bumping into the actor (and Dear Evan Hansen co-star) Ben Platt when he was on a job for Postmates ... and feeling so ashamed that he pretended he was doing something else"). Attributed to the magazine; the quoted words are the writer's. A small, concrete instance of shame about being seen in a lowly state.
claims.alternative: Paraphrase, not a quote from Faist; embarrassment at being caught in a side job is common. The timing relative to Dear Evan Hansen is not stated, so the draft does not call Platt his "future" co-star.

claims.claim: He is adopted; at 17 he met his birth mother's side of the family, "a family of pilots"; after a flight with a relative he thought "Hey, I can do this! That's how we can bond!" and got his pilot's licence, adding "now we bond as a family in a way" (Interview, March 2017). In 2024 he told Esquire a simpler version: "I was impressed with how young they were. And I thought maybe I could do it, too. So I just did it."
claims.passage: He is adopted, and at 17 he met his birth mother's family, "a family of pilots," he told Interview in 2017. After a flight with one of them he thought, "That's how we can bond!" and got his pilot's license.
claims.inference: His own 2017 account gives a relational reason (bonding with newly met relatives); the article cites it as belonging, which the Six case notes, and against Five detachment.
claims.alternative: The 2024 retelling stresses being impressed and doing it on impulse, not bonding; the motive may be mixed. No birth-family member is named and the adoption is not linked to his inner life, per the research do-not-use list.

claims.claim: He made his Broadway debut at 20 in the original cast of Newsies (2012); joined Dear Evan Hansen in its 2015 Arena Stage production as Connor Murphy, stayed through its Broadway opening in December 2016, and earned a 2017 Tony nomination.
claims.passage: Faist made his Broadway debut at 20, in the original cast of _Newsies_ in 2012. In 2015 he joined _Dear Evan Hansen_ at Washington's Arena Stage as Connor Murphy, the troubled teenager whose suicide sets the plot moving, and stayed with it to Broadway, where it opened in December 2016. The role earned him a 2017 Tony nomination.
claims.inference: S05: "He was 20 when he made his Broadway debut in the original cast of 'Newsies'"; "joined the original company of 'Dear Evan Hansen' for a 2015 production at Washington, D.C.'s Arena Stage"; Tony nomination. S11: "opened on Broadway last December" (written December 2017). S32 for the 2012-2013 Newsies run and the nomination category. S35 confirms the 2012 Newsies role.
claims.alternative: None on the facts. Exit date is C12.

claims.claim: He left Dear Evan Hansen in the summer of 2018 and went straight on: he sent his audition tape for Riff, and that November was performing in Steven Levenson's off-Broadway Days of Rage when the call to audition came (Washington Post, Dec. 2021). Asked in 2021 why he was not in the film adaptation, he said "I feel like I couldn't do it," explaining that eight shows a week "very much turns into relying on your technique and the job of it"; he did not say whether he was offered a role.
claims.passage: He left in the summer of 2018, [The Washington Post](https://www.stripes.com/living/entertainment/movies/2021-12-13/faist-actor-west-side-story-profile-entertainment-3955668.html) reported, and kept moving: an audition tape for Riff, then Steven Levenson's off-Broadway play _Days of Rage_. Asked by the Times in 2021 why he was not in the _Dear Evan Hansen_ film, he said, "I feel like I couldn't do it." Eight shows a week, he explained, "very much turns into relying on your technique and the job of it." He did not say whether a film role was offered.
claims.inference: The 2018 exit ended a long run and led directly into new work; it is not evidence of stepping back from momentum. The 2021 answer is about why he did not do the film.
claims.alternative: Fatigue after about three years of eight shows a week explains the film answer as well as any motive; the article draws no type inference from it.

claims.claim: During Dear Evan Hansen he rarely did the stage-door autograph line, signing "maybe twice a week" for repeat customers, because fans "feel like they know us, in a way" and "I don't want to take that away from them, by having them meet who I actually am."
claims.passage: What he guarded hardest was the gap between Connor and himself. He rarely did the stage-door autograph line, he told [MTV News](https://web.archive.org/web/2017/http://www.mtv.com/news/3002027/mike-faist-dear-evan-hansen-interview/) in April 2017, signing only "maybe twice a week" for repeat customers. Fans "feel like they know us, in a way," he said, and "I don't want to take that away from them, by having them meet who I actually am."
claims.inference: MTV (S12, April 26, 2017; the article link points to the Wayback capture used to open it). Verbatim fragments. His concern is that his real self would disappoint or dispel what audiences felt.
claims.alternative: Also a practical boundary for an actor playing a suicidal teenager eight times a week. One source, but it matches his 2026 statements (C36, C92).

claims.claim: From 2017 to 2026 he marks his own craft down, in varied registers: banter at BUILD ("You know, I keep fooling everyone. I really have no idea, it works out," 2017); a skill comparison at the West Side Story dance call ("I'm not an ensemble dancer ... I'm not good enough ... These were some of the best dancers in the world," 2022); and an aspiration on PBS ("I still feel that way. Maybe I'll be good one day. That'd be cool," 2026, recalling being "really excited to get better").
claims.passage: Self-doubt runs through his interviews, often as a joke. Asked at BUILD how he kept landing musicals when he did not consider himself a strong singer, he said, "You know, I keep fooling everyone. I really have no idea, it works out." Of the _West Side Story_ dance call, he told [Screen International](https://www.screendaily.com/features/do-i-have-to-dance-mike-faist-on-moving-from-stage-to-screen-for-west-side-story/5168275.article) in 2022, "I'm not an ensemble dancer," then: "I'm not good enough. I had no business being in that room, quite frankly. These were some of the best dancers in the world." In October 2026, remembering the 17-year-old who was "really excited to get better," he said on [PBS's American Masters](https://www.pbs.org/wnet/americanmasters/podcast/mike-faist-interview/), "I still feel that way. Maybe I'll be good one day. That'd be cool."
claims.inference: Shows a persistent habit of marking his skill down. The article states these are not confessions and, in the Six section, that skill doubt does not discriminate Four from Six.
claims.alternative: Self-deprecation is a common performer register and fits Six self-doubt and Nine self-effacement as well as Four; it is no longer counted toward the Four case.

claims.claim: He told BAFTA in March 2022: "I tend to get anxious or have a bit of anxiety before every project, no matter what it is."
claims.passage: "I tend to get anxious or have a bit of anxiety before every project, no matter what it is."
claims.inference: S19 at 04:27-05:07; wording agrees in both transcriptions. The clip is embedded at that timestamp. Strongest evidence for a fear-centred type.
claims.alternative: Performance anxiety is near universal among actors. The content of this fear is adequacy ("Why did they hire me?", C86), not danger or betrayal (C49).

claims.claim: In September 2026 he described an inner voice urging safety before a yes ("Oh, don't do that. Don't jump into the volcano. Stay up here where it's safe. But, that's the thrill of what we get to do," Cultured); the same dread-and-thrill answer recurs across the East of Eden press cycle (Forbes, PBS, Interview) and is presented once.
claims.passage: In 2026 he described fear as something he chases. "The other tiny voice inside of you goes, Oh, don't do that. Don't jump into the volcano. Stay up here where it's safe," he told Cultured. "But, that's the thrill of what we get to do." A counterphobic Six moves toward what frightens him, though he gave versions of that answer all through one press cycle.
claims.inference: S10 verbatim (opened via Wayback), following "And then the other one is fear, because you don't want to mess up." Versions in S07 (dread, the volcano), S03 ("hell yes and oh shit") and S08 ("dread"). Presented once, not as four observations.
claims.alternative: A repeated junket answer from one press cycle. It can be read as a counterphobic Six or as a Four reading fear as a sign of personal meaning.

claims.claim: He manages anxiety through preparation and trusted leaders: research has been "my way to feel more secure, to feel like I am prepared" since Dear Evan Hansen (Another Man, 2024); a showrunner with a clear vision "helps any sort of anxieties because it's like, well, someone's steering the ship" (PBS, 2026); "The real hope is that you can surround yourself with people, quite frankly, who are a lot smarter than you" (BBC Radio 1, October 2026).
claims.passage: He manages it the way a Six does: research, which he told Another Man is his way "to feel more secure"; a showrunner "steering the ship"; and, he told [BBC Radio 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gMOhYHCmN9w) in October 2026, people "a lot smarter than you."
claims.inference: S01 (research), S03 verbatim (about Zoe Kazan), S21 at 07:09-07:44 (both transcriptions agree; one has "The real hope", the other "you know, the real hope"). Seeking a trustworthy authority to reduce anxiety is a core Six pattern.
claims.alternative: Any actor prefers a director with a plan.

claims.claim: On West Side Story he deliberately built the Jets into a group: "I have to step in here kind of and do something" because "I wanted to actually create a family, a brotherhood, a tribe"; he had each Jet choose an activity everyone had to join, one of which was a LARPing session.
claims.passage: "I wanted to actually create a family, a brotherhood, a tribe," he said, and had each Jet pick an activity the whole gang had to do.
claims.inference: S18 at 09:19-09:55 (both transcriptions agree; the source has "I have to, I have to step in here"; the repetition is dropped at the start of the quotation and the two quoted pieces are separated in the source by "'Cause one, I wanted to create an environment for all of us."). S19 at 09:12-10:23: after the first rehearsal he took the Jets for a drink and "I wanted everyone to come up with an activity and no matter what it was, we all had to do it"; they surprised Kyle Allen at his LARPing group. S15: "We were a family. We were a tribe."
claims.alternative: Ensemble bonding is standard on musicals; he was the senior Jet. Fits Six, Two or Nine group orientation at least as well as Four.

claims.claim: Tony Kushner's favourite memory of the shoot: after the Jets defaced a Puerto Rican flag mural, Faist was among those scrubbing it off, "not in any way done for display ... because he felt terribly about what his character had just done."
claims.passage: Kushner's favorite memory of the shoot was quieter. After the Jets splashed paint over a mural of the Puerto Rican flag, crew members set about scrubbing it off. "One of the people washing it was Mike," he said. "And it really wasn't in any way done for display. It was something that he needed to do because he felt terribly about what his character had just done, and he needed to do something to make himself feel okay about it." The motive is Kushner's reading. The scrubbing is something he watched.
claims.inference: Independent named testimony (S05). Shows conscience and an urge to repair.
claims.alternative: The motive is Kushner’s reading; one anecdote. It could suggest a strong conscience (One, Two, Six) rather than any single type.

claims.claim: He builds and stays loyal to groups: the Jets (C19); his family (C30); a friend he has known since 16, who shared his Columbus house when Another Man visited in 2024; and the first Ohio Artists Gathering, a one-week festival he organised at Short North Stage in Columbus in August 2018 ("I wanted to bring this work to a city I love and call home").
claims.passage: He builds groups and stays loyal to them: the Jets, the family he moved home to help, a high-school friend he lived with in 2024, and the [Ohio Artists Gathering](https://www.columbusunderground.com/gahanna-native-and-tony-nominee-mike-faist-brings-inaugural-ohio-artists-gathering-to-short-north-stage-rs1/), a festival he organized in Columbus in August 2018.
claims.inference: S13 verbatim (the article link points to the live Columbus Underground URL; it was opened through Wayback); S14 corroborates; S09 shows the plan in 2017.
claims.alternative: A career-building and civic project as much as a personal one. No evidence of a second edition was found; the draft does not imply it became annual.

claims.claim: In a New York Times Q&A published May 27, 2021, conducted in Park Slope about seven months before West Side Story opened (December 10, 2021), he called the West Side Story shoot "transcendental: either I didn't feel like I was myself, or I was the most authentic version of myself. I can't really tell which one." His 2024 "vessel" description of the same shoot is C75/C76.
claims.passage: In May 2021, seven months before Steven Spielberg's _West Side Story_ reached theaters, Mike Faist sat down in Park Slope with [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2021/05/27/arts/television/mike-faist-panic-west-side-story.html) and tried to describe what making it had felt like. He called it "transcendental: either I didn't feel like I was myself, or I was the most authentic version of myself. I can't really tell which one."
claims.inference: Verbatim from the NYT answer to "what are you lining up?" (S04, Wayback raw capture). The Park Slope setting and the December release date are from the same article ("a recent sunny morning in Park Slope"; theatrical release Dec. 10). His peak experience is losing himself in the work, which he alternately calls self-loss and most-authentic self.
claims.alternative: This is the hinge between Four (most authentic self) and Nine (merging, self-forgetting); he himself cannot tell. Flow states are common to performers. "Seven months" is approximate (late May to December 10).

claims.claim: In May 2021 he said "Having gone from having no money, wanting to just be a working actor — I don't want to just be a working actor anymore" and "I just don't want to follow the trajectory of what the industry wants me to do," defining that trajectory, when asked "Which is what?", as "Put on a cape and wear a mask." Kushner's independent confirmation of the refusals is C60.
claims.passage: "Having gone from having no money, wanting to just be a working actor — I don't want to just be a working actor anymore," he said. "I just don't want to follow the trajectory of what the industry wants me to do." Asked what that trajectory was, he said, "Put on a cape and wear a mask."
claims.inference: He names the security goal he once had (steady work after having no money) and sets it aside after a transformative job: a dated, first-person statement of trading security for meaning.
claims.alternative: Post-pandemic and post-shoot exhaustion, and his father falling ill that year, could also explain the retreat; the article states that circumstance explains part of the 2021 episode.

claims.claim: In 2024 he described the work he wants: "Like, it's coming from me. Like not necessarily for love, but from love. It may not be good [laughs] but it's coming from that place of 'I'm free, I'm liberated, I'm the most authentic I can be.'"
claims.passage: "Like, it's coming from me. Like not necessarily for love, but from love. It may not be good [laughs] but it's coming from that place of 'I'm free, I'm liberated, I'm the most authentic I can be.'"
claims.inference: Verbatim from S01, continuing C65. The 2021 version is C67 (S05). Authenticity and personal meaning are his stated criteria for work.
claims.alternative: Words, and the familiar vocabulary of prestige-indie actors. The weight comes from the refusals that match them (C12, C60, C35).

claims.claim: He says he would "like to ultimately be of service and of use; that's when I feel at my best" (2021) and "So acting is just constantly giving. You have to be really giving to whatever that person needs" (2026).
claims.passage: He wants to be useful. "I would like to ultimately be of service and of use; that's when I feel at my best," he told the Times in 2021. "So acting is just constantly giving," he said on PBS in 2026.
claims.inference: Two outlets five years apart (2021, 2026).
claims.alternative: A Two-, Six- or Nine-flavoured value that the Four reading does not predict; recorded in "unexplained".

claims.claim: Florence Pugh says that for a later East of Eden scene of only a few lines, which an assistant director would usually read, Faist "insisted on coming back early to be in the room and reading with me," and "what that created was a whole relationship."
claims.passage: Florence Pugh saw that from across a scene. For a later _East of Eden_ moment with only a few lines, which an assistant director would usually read, "he insisted on coming back early to be in the room and reading with me," she told [TV Insider](https://www.tvinsider.com/1294095/east-of-eden-cathy-charles-florence-pugh-mike-faist-interview/). "And what that created was a whole relationship." Kushner's mural story belongs here too.
claims.inference: Co-star testimony about a specific behaviour (S24). "Assistant director" renders her "the first AD". She adds "We put him in more and more."
claims.alternative: Promotional context and a friendly witness; it shows devotion to the work and to a scene partner, not a type.

claims.claim: He left New York at the start of the pandemic and spent much of the next two years driving the country with his rescue dog, Austin, and writing a screenplay.
claims.passage: After the pandemic shutdown he spent much of two years driving the country with his dog, Austin, and writing a screenplay.
claims.inference: S15 (early 2022): "Having left New York at the outset of the pandemic and spent much of the past two years travelling around the US in his car, with his dog". S04 (May 2021): "He spent some of the past year driving around the country with Austin and writing a screenplay."
claims.alternative: The pandemic forced breaks on everyone; road trips with a dog are not a type. He also moved to Ohio in 2021 (C30) and shot Challengers in 2022, so the travel was not continuous.

claims.claim: When his father, Kurt, fell ill with pulmonary fibrosis he moved back to Ohio in 2021 to help care for him and bought a house in Columbus's German Village, which he renovated (almost entirely himself per Another Man; with his father per GQ).
claims.passage: His father, Kurt, had fallen ill with pulmonary fibrosis, and in 2021 Faist moved home to help care for him, buying a house in Columbus that he renovated, partly with his father's help.
claims.inference: S01: returned "in February 2021 when his father got sick"; "bought a house in Columbus's German Village, which he has since renovated almost entirely by himself"; "the house he did up with some help from his dad". S02: "In 2021, just after West Side Story, Faist ... moved back to Ohio to help care for his ailing father ... father and son renovated a house together."
claims.alternative: Many people move home for a sick parent; it shows loyalty and family attachment (compatible with Six, Nine, Two or Four). No month is printed because S01 (February) and S02 ("just after West Side Story") differ.

claims.claim: During the 2024-2026 gap: Sgt. Rock, a DC film he was reportedly attached to with Guadagnino, fell apart "more or less in prep" (Kuritzkes, who calls it "very much a superhero movie that was about everyday heroes, humans, normal people"); he was announced for an off-Broadway Anna Christie opposite Michelle Williams in June 2025 and had withdrawn by August 26, 2025; no reason for the withdrawal was public as of October 2026.
claims.passage: _Sgt. Rock_, a DC film he was reportedly attached to with Guadagnino, fell apart "more or less in prep," its screenwriter Justin Kuritzkes told GQ. A DC film sits oddly with 2021's "cape" line, though Kuritzkes calls it a superhero movie "about everyday heroes, humans, normal people." In June 2025 Faist was announced opposite Michelle Williams in an off-Broadway [_Anna Christie_](https://www.russh.com/anna-christie-mike-faist-michelle-williams). By August 26 he had [withdrawn](https://www.newyorktheatreguide.com/theatre-news/news/tom-sturridge-brian-darcy-james-join-michelle-williams-in-anna-christie-off-broadway). As of October 2026, no reason had been made public.
claims.inference: Part of the gap was outside his control (a collapsed studio film). Reportedly preparing a DC film sits in tension with his 2021 "cape" line. The Anna Christie withdrawal is recorded as unexplained and is not used as evidence of any trait.
claims.alternative: Sgt. Rock attachment is reported only as "reportedly"/rumours; the withdrawal may have been scheduling, health, family or a producer decision.
claims.review_trigger: Update if Faist, the Anna Christie producers or a reliable report gives a reason for the 2025 withdrawal, or if he comments on Sgt. Rock.

claims.claim: In a September 2026 conversation with Jonathan Anderson he said: "I actually feel a lot more comfortable being a character than I do being myself in the public eye. I feel a lot braver, quite frankly, to be someone else."
claims.passage: "I actually feel a lot more comfortable being a character than I do being myself in the public eye. I feel a lot braver, quite frankly, to be someone else."
claims.inference: Verbatim from S08 (two consecutive sentences of one turn, beginning "Part of the reason I don't like doing interviews is that..."). Shame and exposure about the self, not fear of harm, is the emotion named. GQ the same month: "it's a lot easier for me to put on a character and be in front of the world than be me" (S02, carried in metadata by C99).
claims.alternative: Introverted actors often say this; it was a theme of one press cycle. Consistent, though, with 2017 (C14, C70) and the 2026 GQ walk ("a big step", C92).

claims.claim: Zoe Kazan describes "a privacy to Mike ... that I am very careful not to push on" and likens him to "a hermit crab ... There's this shell on the outside and you can't tell what's inside."
claims.passage: Kazan, who told GQ she is "very careful not to push on" his privacy, reached for an animal: "There's something about Mike that reads to me like a hermit crab or something. There's this shell on the outside and you can't tell what's inside."
claims.inference: Independent named testimony from his East of Eden showrunner (S02), verbatim fragments. She continues: "And there's a softness to him, but there's also this kind of toughness ... Like, steely."
claims.alternative: A collaborator promoting the series; "authentic" is her word and a GQ theme. Privacy and a hard shell also fit Five and Six.

claims.claim: Before East of Eden he met Zoe Kazan twice; she recalls him saying, "I don't need you to convince me. I just need to know that this is right for me, because when I jump in, I jump in 100%."
claims.passage: Zoe Kazan, its writer and showrunner, told GQ they met twice before he agreed: "I don't need you to convince me. I just need to know that this is right for me."
claims.inference: Kazan's memory frames the yes as a test of personal fit.
claims.alternative: His own accounts of the same decision credit Kazan's clear vision and the people involved (C107); the article says the decision does not separate Four from Six.

claims.claim: He says he took The Bikeriders "because all I had to do was just be the observer."
claims.passage: He took that one "because all I had to do was just be the observer," he said on PBS.
claims.inference: Verbatim from S03. S01 ("I wanted to be a fly on the wall") and S06 ("on the opposite side of the camera") say the same. The role was the photographer Danny Lyon. His on-set "not about me at all" is C09.
claims.alternative: The role was literally an observer, so the description fits the part. Supports Five (or Nine self-effacement) more than Four.

claims.claim: People who meet him describe easy company: Panic co-star Jessica Sula calls him "so fabulously ridiculous and wonderful"; Jonathan Anderson tells him "You're just a modest person, Mike."
claims.passage: People describe easy company. His co-star on the 2021 Amazon series _Panic_, Jessica Sula, told the Times he is "so fabulously ridiculous and wonderful." Anderson told him, "You're just a modest person, Mike."
claims.inference: S04 ("He's just so fabulously ridiculous and wonderful," she said of Faist) and S08 verbatim.
claims.alternative: Friendly witnesses in promotional settings.

claims.claim: He is playful in public: at the April 2024 Challengers press conference he said he and O'Connor "hate each other" (a running bit); asked by GQ about Oh, Mary!, "I would rock Mary Todd."
claims.passage: He is funny. At the _Challengers_ press conference he announced that he and O'Connor "hate each other." Asked by GQ about playing Mary Todd in _Oh, Mary!_, he said, "I would rock Mary Todd."
claims.inference: S30: "Well, we hate each other." and O'Connor: "we did an interview where he committed so much to this joke that it sounded like I bullied you." S02: "You know what? I would rock Mary Todd. Why not?"
claims.alternative: Junket banter. It complicates a purely melancholic portrait; noted in "unexplained".

claims.claim: In August 2026 GQ found him about to begin rehearsals for the first production he had worked on since East of Eden "two years ago"; he would not say what it was.
claims.passage: By then GQ had found him about to start rehearsals for his first production since _East of Eden_. He would not say what it was.
claims.inference: S02: "Netflix was like, 'We love him so much. We'll pay for another episode,'" says Kazan; "When we meet in August, Faist tells me he's about to enter rehearsals for the first production he's worked on since East of Eden two years ago. True to form, he's tight-lipped about the nature of the production." The East of Eden premiere date is carried by C61.
claims.alternative: Current facts that will change.
claims.review_trigger: Review when the production he began rehearsing in August 2026 is announced or opens, or by 2027-04-01.

claims.claim: Interpretation (type answer): since 2017 he has guarded his plain self from public view (stage door 2017; interviews 2026), and he has turned down work that did not feel like his own (the 2021 refusals Kushner confirms).
claims.passage: Since 2017 he has guarded his plain self from public view, and he has turned down work that didn't feel like his own.
claims.inference: Rests on the dated 2017 stage-door choice, his 2026 statements about being himself in public, and the 2021 refusals. It no longer claims a repeated pattern of stepping back from momentum.
claims.alternative: Privacy and selectiveness are common among prestige actors and also fit Six, Nine and Five readings; the 2018 exit and 2024-26 gap are not counted as chosen withdrawals.
claims.review_trigger: When his next production (rehearsing from August 2026) is announced, or if he takes on back-to-back projects through 2028 or speaks about public life differently, re-test this sentence, the type FAQ and the meta description.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the fear that recurs from 2017 to 2026 is of his plain self being seen: keeping fans from meeting "who I actually am" (MTV 2017), hiding a delivery job from Ben Platt out of shame (Another Man 2024, writer's report), "I'm embarrassed to do this interview" (Interview 2026).
claims.passage: From 2017 to 2026 the fear that recurs is of his plain self being seen: fans kept from meeting "who I actually am," a delivery job hidden from Ben Platt out of shame, "I'm embarrassed to do this interview."
claims.inference: Exposure of the ordinary self, not skill or safety, is the content these passages share; that is the heart-triad shame the Four reading predicts.
claims.alternative: A phobic Six can experience exposure as threat, and Anderson says he gets embarrassed too; the article names the vocabulary baseline and keeps Six close.

claims.claim: FAQ: he was born on January 5, 1992, in Gahanna, Ohio, per IBDB, so he turned 34 in January 2026.
claims.passage: He was born on January 5, 1992, in Gahanna, Ohio, a suburb of Columbus, according to the Internet Broadway Database, so he turned 34 in January 2026.
claims.inference: S31 header "Born Jan 05, 1992 Gahanna, Ohio, USA"; S02 calls him 34 in its September 30, 2026 story. Gahanna is a Columbus suburb (S01, S05).
claims.alternative: Reference-database birth date; every printed age is consistent with it.

claims.claim: FAQ: raised in Gahanna by Kurt and Julie Faist; he has said he is adopted; his mother is Julie in Another Man and Julia elsewhere; his father died December 12, 2023, after three years of pulmonary fibrosis; Faist moved home in 2021 to help care for him.
claims.passage: He was raised in Gahanna, Ohio, by Kurt and Julie Faist, and he has said publicly that he is adopted. Another Man, which interviewed his mother in 2024, calls her Julie; some outlets spell it Julia. His father died on December 12, 2023, after three years of pulmonary fibrosis. Faist had moved home to Ohio in 2021 to help care for him.
claims.inference: S09: "I'm adopted"; S06: raised "by adoptive parents". S01 names Kurt and Julie (she speaks in the piece); S33 (People) says Julia. Father's death: S01 + S33. Move home: S02 ("In 2021 ... moved back to Ohio to help care for his ailing father").
claims.alternative: Birth-family details are deliberately omitted. The name variant is attributed, not reconciled.

claims.claim: Metadata birth_date is 1992-01-05.
claims.inference: IBDB (S31). Not a year turned into January 1: the full date is in the source.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: In New York he dropped out of the American Musical and Dramatic Academy after two semesters and at times lived on food stamps.
claims.passage: He dropped out of the American Musical and Dramatic Academy after two semesters and at times lived on food stamps.
claims.inference: S34 (as-told-to, 2017): "I dropped out after two semesters and started selling tickets in Times Square for off-Broadway plays". S01: "There were times when he was on food stamps"; "selling tickets for Off-Broadway shows to tourists in Times Square". S16: "I went to a conservatory program for two semesters and then I dropped out."
claims.alternative: None on the facts. S09 places food stamps during the Springboro dinner-theatre job; "at times" covers both.

claims.claim: A friend "dragged me kicking and screaming to an audition for White Christmas in Springboro, Ohio at this dinner theater"; booking it gave him "enough confidence to finally go and say, 'I can actually do this.'"
claims.passage: What ended it was another person: "a friend of mine at the time dragged me kicking and screaming to an audition," he told [Interview](https://www.interviewmagazine.com/culture/discovery-mike-faist).
claims.inference: Verbatim from S09 ("THE FIRST JOB"), including "getting paid $150 a week". The nested quotation is double-quoted in the source and set in single quotes here. S16 tells the same sequence ("when I booked that, it gave me enough confidence").
claims.alternative: The friend is unnamed; the push may simply be friendship. Recorded in the Six case (C07) as an outside push resolving a freeze.

claims.claim: The 2021 New York Times piece predicted West Side Story "should put him on Hollywood's speed dial" and reported that he had been turning down offers and was selling his Brooklyn apartment and heading back to Ohio; Another Man and GQ tie the 2021 move to his father falling ill.
claims.passage: The paper predicted the film would put him "on Hollywood's speed dial." He was turning down offers anyway, and selling his Brooklyn apartment to head back to Ohio, where his father had fallen ill.
claims.inference: The reporter's own framing in S04: "should put him on Hollywood's speed dial when it debuts in December"; "He has been turning down offers and is now selling his Brooklyn apartment and heading back to Ohio." Another Man (S01) independently says he sold his Brooklyn flat and bought a house in German Village.
claims.alternative: Reporter's account, not his words; the move also coincides with the pandemic and his father's illness (C29, C30). Which offers he declined is not specified.

claims.claim: Tony Kushner says friends making films after West Side Story asked whether Faist would take parts and "in both cases he turned them down ... the stuff that they were asking just didn't feel right to him at the moment, and it had nothing to do with size of the role."
claims.passage: After the film came out, Kushner told [GQ](https://www.gq.com/story/mike-faist-gq-hype) in 2026, friends making movies called him to ask whether Faist would take this part or that part. "And I think in both cases he turned them down. And he was very nice about it, but the stuff that they were asking just didn't feel right to him at the moment, and it had nothing to do with size of the role or anything."
claims.inference: S02 verbatim; the first sentence paraphrases Kushner's "Two or three people, friends of mine who were making movies after West Side Story came out, called about, 'What's Mike Faist like? Do you think he would do this part or that part?'" Independent named testimony five years after his own 2021 account (C25, C59).
claims.alternative: Kushner is a collaborator and friend; "didn't feel right to him" is Kushner's reading of Faist's reasons.

claims.claim: Career outline: originated Connor Murphy in Dear Evan Hansen; played Riff, leader of the Jets, in West Side Story (2021), earning a BAFTA nomination; Art Donaldson in Challengers (released 2024) opposite Zendaya and Josh O'Connor; Charles Trask ("a quiet farmer who's dangerous when provoked," Cultured) in Netflix's East of Eden, shot about two years before August 2026 per GQ; no new production between that shoot and August 2026; Netflix premiered the series on October 1, 2026.
claims.passage: Faist, born in 1992 and raised in Gahanna, Ohio, originated Connor Murphy in _Dear Evan Hansen_ and played Riff, leader of the Jets, for Spielberg, earning a BAFTA nomination. He was Art Donaldson in _Challengers_ (2024), opposite [Zendaya](/personality-analysis/zendaya) and Josh O'Connor, and plays Charles Trask, a quiet farmer who is dangerous when provoked, in Netflix's _East of Eden_, from John Steinbeck's novel. After shooting it, around 2024, he worked on nothing new for about two years. The series premiered on October 1, 2026.
claims.inference: Left Dear Evan Hansen "in the summer of 2018" (S05). Art Donaldson opposite Zendaya and O'Connor (S02). GQ, August 2026: "about to enter rehearsals for the first production he's worked on since East of Eden two years ago" (S02); Cultured: "looking back, it was two years [without acting]" (S07). Premiere: TV Insider "Series Premiere, October 1, Netflix" (S36) and "Streaming Now" on October 1 (S24).
claims.alternative: He still did 2024 promotion (C82), so this is a gap in new work, not a disappearance from view. The break overlaps grief for his father and the collapse of Sgt. Rock (C35).

claims.claim: The "braver" line answered why he dislikes interviews ("Part of the reason I don't like doing interviews is that..."), in a conversation with Jonathan Anderson that Interview published on October 6, 2026; Anderson costumed Challengers, where they met and became friends.
claims.passage: Explaining why he dislikes interviews to his friend Jonathan Anderson, the designer who costumed _Challengers_, he put it this way in a conversation [Interview](https://www.interviewmagazine.com/film/a-reluctant-interview-between-mike-faist-and-jonathan-anderson) published on October 6, 2026:
claims.inference: S08 published time 2026-10-06; dateline "THURSDAY 2:30 PM SEPTEMBER 17, 2026 PARIS". Friendship: S08 ("We ended up being friends ever since") and S01 ("a great guy and a great friend").
claims.alternative: None on the facts. The friend-to-friend format is less guarded but also playful (S08 context).

claims.claim: Interpretation, limited to the one episode with a stated inward reason: in 2021, at peak demand, he named the security goal he had held since having no money and set it aside, and Kushner independently confirms the refusals were not about the size of the roles. This suggests the Four trade of security for keeping the work his own.
claims.passage: It also leads on what he gave up. A security-first reading predicts that an actor who once had no money takes the safe offers after a hit. In 2021 Faist named that goal, "wanting to just be a working actor," and set it aside, and Kushner independently confirms the refusals had "nothing to do with size of the role." This suggests the Four's trade: security given up to keep the work his own.
claims.inference: A dated first-person statement plus independent testimony about refusals at the moment of most demand; the article marks it "This suggests".
claims.alternative: Exhaustion, the pandemic and his father falling ill coincide with 2021; the article says circumstance explains part of every episode. The 2018 exit, the Brooklyn sale and the 2024-26 gap are explicitly not counted, partly because in August 2026 he said projects "don't happen because of the industry and financing ... There's no control in this industry" (C108) and called Challengers "very overwhelming" (C84).

claims.claim: He has said since 2021 that his work must come from love: "For me, it has to come from a place of passion and love" (Washington Post, December 2021), restated in 2024 (C26, C65).
claims.passage: a rule for choosing work, repeated since 2021, that it has to come from "a place of passion and love."
claims.inference: S05: "For me, it has to come from a place of passion and love." and "If it's anything short of that, I don't know if it's worth it." S01 (2024): "pieces that come from a place of love".
claims.alternative: The familiar vocabulary of prestige-indie actors; the weight comes from the refusals that match it (C48).

claims.claim: Interpretation: since at least 2017 (MTV stage door) through 2026 (Interview, GQ) he has said that being himself in public is harder than being someone else.
claims.passage: Since at least 2017 he has said that being himself in public is harder than being someone else.
claims.inference: Built from the 2017 MTV autograph-line answer (C14, C70), the 2026 Interview and GQ lines (C36, C92), and the reasons he gave in 2021 and 2026 (C25, C83, C84, C38).
claims.alternative: Reticence about press is common; the inward reasons are his own accounts and partly the vocabulary of prestige actors.

claims.claim: Interpretation: anxiety is the feeling he reports most consistently across his interviews.
claims.passage: The feeling he reports most often is anxiety
claims.inference: From C07, C16, C86 and C17: "too scared" (2017), "anxiety before every project" (2022), "We're always nervous" (2023), dread and fear (2026).
claims.alternative: Performance anxiety is near universal among actors; the content of the fear is the discriminator (C49, C87).

claims.claim: He told MTV in 2017: "I just would hate for that illusion to be broken by having interaction with me, that, maybe, [fans] were expecting something else."
claims.passage: "I just would hate for that illusion to be broken by having interaction with me, that, maybe, [fans] were expecting something else."
claims.inference: Verbatim from S12 including MTV's bracketed insertion; the source continues ", almost in a way..." which is cut at a clause boundary.
claims.alternative: One interview; see C14.

claims.claim: In 2017, describing Evan and Connor, he said "they don't want people to see them because if we allow ourselves to be seen, actually seen, and allow [ourselves] to be vulnerable, then we lose the game," followed by "Teens don't want to let people know how they are actually feeling"; the "we" is generational, not a self-disclosure.
claims.passage: That spring he described Evan and Connor to Interview, and the pronoun slid from "they" to "we": "they don't want people to see them because if we allow ourselves to be seen, actually seen, and allow [ourselves] to be vulnerable, then we lose the game." His next sentence made the "we" generational: "Teens don't want to let people know how they are actually feeling." It was not a confession, but he would later say much the same of himself.
claims.inference: Shows the being-seen theme in his vocabulary in 2017; the article states it is not a confession and links it only to his later first-person statements (C36, C92).
claims.alternative: It is a description of his characters and his generation; it carries no weight in the type hypothesis (removed from for_claim_ids).

claims.claim: He went into West Side Story fearing Spielberg would be "a dictator" and the production "Hollywood overproduced," with the actor "just a prop"; instead "Steven never made me feel I needed to ask permission to do anything."
claims.passage: Faist went into _West Side Story_ fearing Spielberg would be "a dictator," he told [Gold Derby](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R1377wu21GE) in December 2021, and the shoot "Hollywood overproduced," with the actor reduced to a prop. Instead, he told [Esquire](https://www.esquire.com/uk/culture/film/a61081999/mike-faist-the-bikeriders-interview/) in 2024, "Steven never made me feel I needed to ask permission to do anything."
claims.inference: S18 at 21:50-22:24 ("I was in fear that he would be, you know, not, you know, a dictator. I thought the whole thing would be, you know, Hollywood overproduced. We're an actor. You're just a prop."); wording agrees in both transcriptions; "reduced to a prop" paraphrases "You're just a prop" and S19's "just be the prop". S06 verbatim.
claims.alternative: Nervousness about a first studio film is ordinary. The fear is of losing his voice, not of harm (C49); it is also read as Six-style wariness of authority (C87).

claims.claim: The moment Riff presses his temple to a gun barrel was unscripted and his idea ("I think I have this idea. Just go with me on it. If you hate it, tell me."); Kushner: "What Mike came up with in that moment is the whole character in this one little gesture."
claims.passage: On camera, he had the unscripted idea of Riff pressing his temple to the barrel of a bartender's gun. "What Mike came up with in that moment," the screenwriter Tony Kushner told the Post, "is the whole character in this one little gesture."
claims.inference: S18 at 18:36-19:41: "I went over to Steven and Tony. I said, I think I have this idea. Just go with me on it. If you hate it, tell me" (both transcriptions agree on the quoted words; one adds "let's try it"); the bartender is played by Jamie Harris. S05: "It was an unscripted choice, Kushner says"; Kushner's quote verbatim.
claims.alternative: An actor's choice in one scene; it shows initiative and instinct, not a type.

claims.claim: In 2024 he described the West Side Story shoot: "It felt like: I'm not me right now, I'm being used to tell the story in the best way possible."
claims.passage: Faist's own description of that shoot is the most revealing thing in his record. "It felt like: I'm not me right now, I'm being used to tell the story in the best way possible," he told Another Man in 2024.
claims.inference: Verbatim from S01 (preceded by "It felt transcendental," he says).
claims.alternative: Calling it "the most revealing thing" is the author's judgment. Flow states are common to performers.

claims.claim: He continued: "It was like being used as a vessel, and that was the best feeling ever."
claims.passage: "It was like being used as a vessel, and that was the best feeling ever."
claims.inference: Verbatim from S01; it follows "I don't know how to explain it, it was like I had no control over the situation." in the same quotation.
claims.alternative: Hinge between Four (most authentic self) and Nine (self-forgetting).

claims.claim: Interpretation: in 2021 he could not say whether the West Side Story state was losing himself or finding himself; that question separates the Four and Nine readings and he has not settled it.
claims.passage: In 2021 he could not decide whether that state was losing himself or finding himself. That question is where the Four and Nine readings part, and he has never settled it.
claims.inference: From C23 ("I can't really tell which one") and C75/C76. "Never settled" means no later source found resolves it.
claims.alternative: A later interview could settle it; the claim is limited to the record opened (through October 2026).

claims.claim: After West Side Story he made Challengers with Luca Guadagnino and played the photographer Danny Lyon in The Bikeriders alongside Austin Butler and Tom Hardy.
claims.passage: _Challengers_ with Luca Guadagnino, then _The Bikeriders_, as the photographer Danny Lyon, alongside [Austin Butler](/personality-analysis/austin-butler) and [Tom Hardy](/personality-analysis/tom-hardy)
claims.inference: S01: Challengers from Luca Guadagnino; The Bikeriders featuring Austin Butler, Jodie Comer and Tom Hardy; he plays Danny Lyon. S06 confirms the role. "By his own rules" refers to C60 and C65.
claims.alternative: None on the facts.

claims.claim: His father died on December 12, 2023, of a blood clot after three years of pulmonary fibrosis, and his grandfather died weeks later ("a month later," Another Man; "within three weeks," GQ, "right before the release of Challengers"); he says "All the men have passed."
claims.passage: His father died on December 12, 2023, and his grandfather weeks later. "All the men have passed," he told GQ.
claims.inference: S01 gives December 12 and the cause; S33 supplies the year 2023; S01 says the grandfather died "A month later" and S02 "within three weeks", so "weeks later". Quote verbatim from S02.
claims.alternative: None on the facts; the grandfather interval is left unreconciled.

claims.claim: Challengers opened in April 2024; Another Man reported he was dreading the press tour; he did the promotion, and in 2024 Anderson put him on the Met Gala carpet in a custom look (Cultured).
claims.passage: _Challengers_ opened in April 2024. He dreaded the press tour, Another Man reported, but did it, and walked the Met Gala carpet in a custom look from Anderson.
claims.inference: S01: "He's dreading the Challengers press tour". S28 and S30: he did the April 23, 2024 junket and press conference with Zendaya and O'Connor. S07: Anderson put him in a Loewe campaign and on the 2024 Met Gala carpet. Gap in new work: C61.
claims.alternative: Dreading press is common among actors.

claims.claim: He explained the gap in GQ (August 2026): "there's a moment of just needing to recalibrate probably for myself ... There's so much noise in this industry and in the world"; "I don't think that I have that kind of stamina. I'm not necessarily a marathon runner."
claims.passage: In GQ he described "needing to recalibrate" amid "so much noise" and said, "I don't think that I have that kind of stamina."
claims.inference: Verbatim from S02 (two consecutive quoted pieces around "he continues"). He also says "there's a moment of just needing to recalibrate probably for myself."
claims.alternative: "Stamina" is equally Nine or Five language (C89).

claims.claim: Asked by Cultured (September 2026) whether he wanted to take a beat, he first said "You know, there really isn't a lot of thought," then that it is easy "to get swept up in noise," making it hard "to really listen, just being able to hear myself think, and feel what is right for me"; "maybe there was an aspect of trying to tune everything out"; "The truth is that Challengers was a lot. It was very overwhelming"; and, later in the answer, "I don't really know how much control I actually have over any of this."
claims.passage: To Cultured, his first answer was, "You know, there really isn't a lot of thought." Then he spoke of needing to "hear myself think, and feel what is right for me," and of "trying to tune everything out." "The truth is that Challengers was a lot. It was very overwhelming," he said. And: "I don't really know how much control I actually have over any of this."
claims.inference: His own account of the gap mixes an inward need for quiet with overwhelm and lack of control; the article presents it as pointing several ways and, in the Nine section, says it fits a Nine as well.
claims.alternative: "Tune everything out" and "allow things to be quiet" are Nine-like signals; the overwhelm followed two family deaths and a sudden jump in fame.

claims.claim: Circumstance explains part of every step back (the pandemic, his father's illness, Sgt. Rock collapsing), and he has never given a reason for leaving Anna Christie.
claims.passage: Circumstance explains part of every episode: the pandemic, his father's illness, a studio film collapsing. And he has never said why he left _Anna Christie_.
claims.inference: From C29, C30 and C35. "Never said" is limited to the sources opened through October 15, 2026.
claims.alternative: A reason could emerge (see C35 review trigger).
claims.review_trigger: Update if a reason for the 2025 Anna Christie withdrawal becomes public.

claims.claim: In the same 2022 BAFTA answer: "I'm always like, oh my God, what did I sign myself up for? I can't do this. Why did they hire me? What are we thinking? What are we doing here? I always like have this awful, awful thing in my whole body before like starting any sort of project." The printed segment ("what did I sign myself up for? I can't do this. Why did they hire me?") matches both local transcriptions; the second transcription has an extra "why," before "what did I", so the quote starts after it.
claims.passage: Each time, he went on, he asks himself "what did I sign myself up for? I can't do this. Why did they hire me?"
claims.inference: A run of worst-case doubts about a commitment already made; the article counts it for the Six case, not the Four.
claims.alternative: Pre-project nerves are common among actors; the question "Why did they hire me?" also reads as adequacy doubt.

claims.claim: Interpretation: asked by GQ whether the grind of promotion was the problem, he named "the public gaze" and the lost anonymity in which "you could kind of be whoever you wanted to be" and be "even more honest" with strangers: a loss of self-expression more than of safety. Apart from the pre-West Side Story worry about Spielberg, he almost never voices suspicion of particular people.

type_hypothesis.against: (1) Anxiety is his most consistent self-report across a decade: six to eight months without auditioning because he "felt too incapable" (2017, C07); "anxiety before every project, no matter what it is ... what did I sign myself up for? I can't do this. Why did they hire me?" (2022, C16, C86); "We're always nervous" (2023, C106); an inner voice saying "Stay up here where it's safe" before every yes (2026, C17). That run of questions is a worst-case worry about a commitment already made (C114). (2) He names security as the purpose of preparation ("research has been my way to feel more secure", C18) and leans on clear leaders and trusted people: his own account of the East of Eden yes is "honestly Zoe and Florence" and a showrunner who is "steering the ship" (C107); "surround yourself with people ... a lot smarter than you" (C18); trusting a director "had cast them for a reason" (C106). (3) He builds and stays loyal to groups: the Jets as "a family, a brotherhood, a tribe" (C19), the Ohio Artists Gathering (C21), a friend since 16 he lived with in 2024 (C21), moving home in 2021 to help care for his father (C30), learning to fly "to bond" with newly met relatives (C09); and "be of service and of use" (C27), coming back early to read for a scene partner (C28). (4) Skill doubts ("I keep fooling everyone", "I'm not good enough", "Maybe I'll be good one day", C15) fit Six self-doubt as well as Four deficiency (C116). (5) The authenticity vocabulary ("from love", "right for me", "braver ... to be someone else") is house language for prestige actors; Anderson describes his own "me on and ... me off" in the same conversation (C112). (6) Nine signals are strong: the vessel as his best experience (C76), "noise", "stamina", "tune everything out", "allow things to be quiet", "there really isn't a lot of thought" (C83, C84, C89), a planned break to "allow myself to be bored" (C89), modesty and easy company (C43), almost no recorded conflict (C88). (7) Circumstance explains part of every episode: the pandemic, his father's illness and death, an overwhelming 2024, a studio film collapsing in prep and an industry where projects die over financing (C29, C30, C35, C80, C84, C108). (8) Several episodes once read as withdrawals are not: the 2018 Dear Evan Hansen exit led straight into the Riff audition and Days of Rage (C12); the 2021 Brooklyn sale was a move home to a sick father (C59, C30); in 2023 he took a West End stage run during his father's illness (C106); he did the 2024 press tour, a Loewe campaign and the Met Gala (C82, C117); in 2026 he says he wants to return to the theater (C110).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 6 is the strongest rival and explains a large share of the record: decade-long anxiety managed by preparation, clear leaders, trusted people and close groups (C07, C16, C17, C18, C19, C21, C86, C106, C107, C114); a friend's push ending his early freeze (C56); the East of Eden yes, which he credits to Kazan's clear lead and the people involved (C107); loyalty to home and old friends (C21, C30); ambivalence about acting itself (C91); and a counterphobic pull toward what frightens him, presented once as a press-cycle answer (C17). What strains the Six reading: the fear that recurs from 2017 to 2026 is about his plain self being seen, not safety, backing or other people's reliability (C14, C70, C36, C49, C92); asked what fame cost him he named lost anonymity and the freedom to "be whoever you wanted to be", not safety (C87, C108); apart from a pre-West Side Story worry about Spielberg he almost never voices suspicion of particular people (C73, C87); and in 2021, at peak demand, he named the security goal of being "just a working actor" and set it aside, while Kushner independently confirms the refusals had "nothing to do with size of the role" (C25, C60, C63). Type 9 is a close second alternative: self-forgetting as peak experience, need for quiet, low stamina, modesty, little recorded conflict (C76, C83, C84, C89, C43, C88). The only lean toward Four over Nine is that he frames the quiet as protecting a self ("hear myself think", "be whoever you wanted to be") rather than peace, and the article concedes a Nine could say the same (C113). Type 5 was considered for the observer stance and privacy and set aside for his group-building and his relational reason for learning to fly (C104). Type 1 was considered for the conscience Kushner describes (C20) and set aside for lack of any sign of a correcting inner critic.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: Two person-specific, dated observations carry the Four lead, each with stated limits. (1) What he guards: from 2017 to 2026 the recurring fear is of his ordinary self being seen, not of his skill failing or of losing support. In April 2017 he limited the stage door so fans would not "meet who I actually am" and break "that illusion" of Connor (C14, C70); in 2026 he says he feels "braver ... to be someone else", "I'm embarrassed to do this interview", and "it's a lot easier for me to put on a character and be in front of the world than be me" (C36, C49, C92); asked whether promotion was the problem, he named "the public gaze" and the lost anonymity in which he could "be whoever you wanted to be" and be "even more honest" with strangers, a loss of self-expression more than of security (C87, C108). (2) What he gave up: in May 2021, at peak demand, he named the security goal he had held since having "no money", being "just a working actor", and set it aside (C25), and Kushner independently confirms he turned down parts for reasons that "had nothing to do with size of the role" (C60, C63). Limits: skill doubt does not discriminate (C116); the authenticity vocabulary is an actor baseline (C112); the East of Eden yes splits between Kazan's test of fit and his own credit to her clear lead (C38, C107, C115); the 2018 exit, the Brooklyn sale and the 2024-2026 gap are mixed or circumstantial and are not counted (C111, C85); the Anna Christie withdrawal has no known reason and is not used (C35); Four and Nine are not yet separated (C113). Settle signals: (a) an account of him in open conflict or let down by a collaborator: a Six would look for allies or a trusted authority and grow wary of the person, a Four would hold to his own sense of what is true at a cost to his standing (C88); (b) how he explains choosing the production he began rehearsing in August 2026: trusted people and a clear leader (Six), "right for me" fit (Four), or a need for quiet and low friction (Nine). Confidence therefore stays medium.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: (1) His instinct to gather and serve people: the Jets, a hometown festival, "be of service and of use; that's when I feel at my best", reading for a scene partner (C19, C21, C27, C28), which sits more naturally with Six, Two or Nine than Four. (2) Kushner's account of him scrubbing paint off the mural because he "felt terribly about what his character had just done" (C20): conscience and repair. (3) The playfulness observers stress more than any melancholy (C43, C44).
